questions.q: According to this lesson, what is data classification?
options: Sorting data into sensitivity tiers so handling rules can apply consistently and automatically
Encrypting every dataset in an organization at the same strength
Deleting data once it reaches a certain age
A legal requirement that only applies to healthcare organizations
questions.explain: Classification assigns a sensitivity label to data so that access, encryption, retention, and sharing rules attach automatically, instead of being decided case by case.

questions.q: Why can't an organization simply apply the strictest possible security controls to all of its data?
options: It's technically impossible to encrypt more than one dataset at a time
It would be extremely costly and slow, over-protecting low-value data that never needed it
Strict controls are illegal under GDPR
Strict controls only work on structured data, not files
questions.explain: Applying maximum controls everywhere is safe but expensive and slow — it burdens low-risk data (like public marketing material) with costs and friction it never needed.

questions.q: What is the risk of applying the same light, average-level controls to all data instead of classifying it?
options: The organization's most sensitive data — like health records or SSNs — ends up with the same casual handling as harmless data
It becomes impossible to back up any data at all
It automatically violates SOX regardless of data content
It makes data permanently unreadable
questions.explain: Light, uniform controls are cheap and fast but leave the genuinely high-risk data — the data that most needs strong protection — under-protected.

questions.q: How does classification connect to Chapter 1's concept of 'sensitive vs. confidential' data?
options: It replaces that concept entirely with a new, unrelated idea
It turns that abstract distinction into a concrete label (e.g., Confidential, Restricted) stamped on an actual dataset
It only applies to data that is neither sensitive nor confidential
It has no relationship to Chapter 1 at all
questions.explain: Classification is the operational bridge: Chapter 1 established which kinds of data carry risk; classification labels make that risk visible and actionable on real datasets.

questions.q: What does this lesson say comes next in Chapter 2, right after classification concepts?
options: Access control and least privilege
Encryption and key management
The common classification schemes and labels organizations actually use
Regulatory requirements under GDPR and HIPAA
questions.explain: Lesson 8 covers classification schemes and labels, followed by discovery (Lesson 9), applying classifications (Lesson 10), and classification governance (Lesson 11).
